documentNotes.title: Full native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface This publication contains 39 theoretical and 14 practical competition problems from the 41st – 45th International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 2009 – 2013. It has been published by the IChO International Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) as a continuation of the preceding Volumes 1 and 2 published on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of the IChO with the titles: • The competition problems from the International Chemistry Olympiads, Volume 1, 1st – 20th IChO, 1968 – 1988 (IUVENTA, Bratislava, 2008). • The competition problems from the International Chemistry Olympiads, Volume 2, 21st – 40th IChO, 1989 – 2008 (IUVENTA, Bratislava, 2009). Not less than 318 theoretical and 110 practical problems were set in the IChO during the forty-five years of its existence. In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems (numbering the tasks of the particular problems, solution inserted immediately after the text of the problem, solutions without grading points and special graphs used for grading of practical problems). Nevertheless, the mentioned corrections and changes do not concern the contents and language of the competition problems. The practical problems set in the IChO competitions, contain as a rule some instructions, list of apparatuses available, chemicals on each desk and those available in the laboratory, and the risk and safety phrases with regard to the chemicals used. All of these items are important for the competitors during the competition but less important for those who are going to read the competition tasks of this collection and thus, they are omitted. Some parts of the solutions of practical problems are also left out since they require the experimental data which could be obtained by experiments during the practical part of the IChO competition. In this publication SI quantities and units are preferred. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI. Although the numbers of significant figures in the results of some solutions do not obey the criteria generally accepted, they were left without change.

Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and due to the procedure of creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to assign any author's name to a particular problem. Nevertheless, responsibility for the scientific content and language of the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry Olympiads. This review of the competition problems from the 41st – 45th IChO should serve to both competitors and their teachers as a source of further ideas in their preparation for this difficult competition. For those who have taken part in some of these International Chemistry Olympiads the collection of the problems could be of help as archival and documentary material. In the previous forty-five years many known and unknown people - teachers, authors, pupils, and organizers proved their abilities and knowledge and contributed to the success of this already well known and world-wide competition. We wish to all who will organize and attend the future International Chemistry Olympiads, success and happiness. Bratislava, July 2014 Anton Sirota, editor

Source note: The Washington2012 section prints practical chemical lists, procedures, blank recording/answer forms, mechanisms and evaluation conditions; all are retained. Referenced but absent answer boxes, exact stock-label values, original score allocations, data-dependent results and separate answer sheets are not invented.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 1 — Boron Hydrides and Other Boron Compounds
problems.statement:
**A. Boron Hydrides and Other Boron Compounds**

Boron hydride chemistry was first developed by Alfred Stock (1876–1946). More than 20 neutral molecular boron hydrides with general formula BₓHᵧ have been characterized. The simplest is B₂H₆, diborane.

[figure: p1-fig1]

parts.statement:
Using the following data derive molecular formulae for boron hydrides A and B.

| Substance | State (25 °C, 1 bar) | Mass percent boron | Molar mass / g mol⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Liquid | 83.1 | 65.1 |
| B | Solid | 88.5 | 122.2 |
parts.statementAfter:
William Lipscomb received the 1976 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studies on boron-hydride structures illuminating chemical bonding. In all boron hydrides each B atom has a normal 2-electron bond to at least one H atom (B–H). Additional bond types occur. His styx number describes a borane:

- s: number of B–H–B bridges.
- t: number of 3-center BBB bonds.
- y: number of two-center B–B bonds.
- x: number of BH₂ groups.

[figure: p1-fig2]

The styx number for B₂H₆ is 2002.

parts.statement: Propose a structure for tetraborane B₄H₁₀ with styx number 4012.

A boron-based compound contains boron, carbon, chlorine and oxygen. Spectra indicate tetrahedral and trigonal planar B atoms in a 1:3 ratio and are consistent with a CO triple bond. Its molecular formula is B₄CCl₆O. Suggest its molecular structure.
parts.statementAfter: **B. Thermochemistry of Boron Compounds**

parts.statement:
Estimate the B–B single-bond dissociation enthalpy in B₂Cl₄(g) using:

| Bond | Dissociation enthalpy / kJ mol⁻¹ |
|---|---|
| B–Cl | 443 |
| Cl–Cl | 242 |

| Compound | ΔfH° / kJ mol⁻¹ |
|---|---|
| BCl₃(g) | −403 |
| B₂Cl₄(g) | −489 |
parts.statementAfter: **C. Chemistry of Diborane**

parts.statement:
Give the structure of each numbered boron-containing compound in the following scheme.

[figure: p1-fig3]

Notes: (i) Compound 5 boils at 55 °C. (ii) Excess reagents are used in all reactions. (iii) 0.312 g of compound 2 in 25.0 g benzene causes freezing-point depression 0.205 °C; benzene’s depression constant is 5.12 kg K mol⁻¹.

solution.statement:
**1.1** A = B₅H₁₁; B = B₁₀H₁₄.

**1.2** Actual structure and unknown but acceptable structure:

[figure: p1-sol-fig1]

**1.3** Proposed structure:

[figure: p1-sol-fig2]

**1.4** Native Born–Haber cycle:

[figure: p1-sol-fig3]

A Born–Haber cycle gives B–B bond dissociation enthalpy 327 kJ mol⁻¹.

**1.5** Complete formula/structure table:

[figure: p1-sol-fig4]

1: B(OCH₃)₃. 2: B₃O₃(C₆H₅)₃; dimers/tetramers [C₆H₅BO]ₓ (x = 2, 4) are also acceptable. 3: BCl₃. 4: BNH₆ and 5: B₃N₃H₆; formal charges are not necessary for 4/5.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 2 — Platinum(II) Compounds, Isomers, and the Trans Effect
problems.statement:
**A. Platinum(II) Compounds, Isomers, and the Trans Effect**

Platinum and other Group 10 metals form square planar complexes; their reaction mechanisms have been extensively studied. Substitution proceeds with retention of stereochemistry:

[figure: p2-fig1]

The rate of replacing X by Y depends on ligand T trans to X (the trans effect). For the following T ligands the trans substitution rate decreases left to right:

CN⁻ > H⁻ > NO₂⁻, I⁻ > Br⁻, Cl⁻ > pyridine, NH₃, OH⁻, H₂O.

Preparations of cis- and trans-Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂ depend on this effect (source writes “trans affect”). The cis isomer, the cancer chemotherapy agent cisplatin, is prepared by reacting K₂PtCl₄ with ammonia.

[figure: p2-fig2]

parts.statement: Draw all possible stereoisomers of square planar Pt(py)(NH₃)BrCl, with py = pyridine C₅H₅N.
Write aqueous reaction schemes, including any intermediates, preparing each stereoisomer of [Pt(NH₃)(NO₂)Cl₂]⁻ from PtCl₄²⁻, NH₃ and NO₂⁻, controlled kinetically by the trans effect.
parts.statementAfter:
**B. Kinetic Studies of Substitution Reactions of Square Planar Complexes**

ML₃X + Y → ML₃Y + X can proceed by either or both mechanisms:

i) Direct substitution: Y attaches to the central metal to form five-coordinate ML₃XY, then rapidly eliminates X. Formation is rate-determining with rate constant kY.

ML₃X —(+Y; rate-determining, kY)→ [ML₃XY] —(−X)→ ML₃Y.

ii) Solvent-assisted substitution: solvent S attaches to form ML₃XS, which eliminates X to give ML₃S; Y rapidly displaces S. Solvent attachment is rate-determining with constant kS.

ML₃X —(+S; rate-determining, kS)→ [ML₃XS] —(−X)→ [ML₃S] —(+Y; −S)→ ML₃Y.

Rate = kS[ML₃X] + kY[Y][ML₃X]. When [Y] ≫ [ML₃X], Rate = kobs[ML₃X]. Values kS/kY depend on reactants/solvent. One example is displacement of Cl⁻ in square planar ML₂X₂ by pyridine; the ML₃X scheme also applies to ML₂X₂.

[figure: p2-fig3]

At 25 °C in methanol, [pyridine] ≫ platinum-complex concentration:

| [Pyridine] / mol dm⁻³ | kobs / s⁻¹ |
|---|---|
| 0.122 | 7.20×10⁻⁴ |
| 0.061 | 3.45×10⁻⁴ |
| 0.030 | 1.75×10⁻⁴ |

parts.statement: Calculate kS and kY with proper units. A grid is given if you wish to use it. Source gap: the optional grid is not printed in this obtained collection.

For [pyridine] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, tick the correct answer:

- Most pyridine product forms by solvent-assisted (kS) substitution.
- Most forms by direct (kY) substitution.
- Comparable product amounts form by both pathways.
- No conclusion about relative amounts can be drawn.
parts.statementAfter:
**C. A chemotherapy agent**

To better target cisplatin to cancer cells, Professor Lippard’s MIT group attached a platinum(IV) complex to oligonucleotides bound to gold nanoparticles.

[figure: p2-fig4]

parts.statement: Gold nanoparticles have diameter 13 nm and 90 attached oligonucleotide groups, 98% bound to a Pt(IV) complex. A reaction vessel treating cells has volume 1.0 cm³ and 1.0×10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ platinum concentration. Calculate the platinum and gold masses used. Gold density 19.3 g cm⁻³; sphere volume (4/3)πr³ = 4.18879r³.

solution.statement:
**2.1** Three stereoisomers:

[figure: p2-sol-fig1]

**2.2** Cis- and trans-isomer preparation schemes:

[figure: p2-sol-fig2]

Source note: The trans scheme prints the Pt(NO₂)Cl₃ intermediate charge 2−; that printed charge is retained.

**2.3**

[figure: p2-sol-fig3]

Fig. 2.3 verifies the rate law kobs = kS + kY[pyridine] for Pt(bipy)Cl₂ → Pt(bipy)(py)Cl⁺. Data credit L. Cattalini, A. Orio, A. Doni, Inorg. Chem. 5, 1517 (1966).

kY = 5.8×10⁻³ s⁻¹ mol⁻¹ dm³; kS = 0 s⁻¹. Allow a small range ±0.2×10⁻³ for kS.

**2.4** Most pyridine product forms by direct (kY) substitution.

**2.5 — Platinum:** n(Pt) = 1.0×10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ × 0.001 dm³ = 1.0×10⁻⁹ mol, equivalent to 2.0×10⁻⁷ g Pt.

**Gold:** 90 groups/particle × 0.98 Pt-bound complexes = 88 Pt complexes (88 atoms) per nanoparticle. 1.0×10⁻⁹ mol Pt is 6.0×10¹⁴ atoms. Thus 6.0×10¹⁴ / 88 = 6.8×10¹² nanoparticles.

Radius 6.5×10⁻⁷ cm; nanoparticle volume 1.2×10⁻¹⁸ cm³, mass 2.3×10⁻¹⁷ g, gold amount 1.2×10⁻¹⁹ mol and 7.1×10⁴ atoms. Total gold atoms = (6.8×10¹² particles)(7.1×10⁴ atoms/particle) = 4.8×10¹⁷, equivalent to 1.5×10⁻⁴ g Au.

figures.alt: All three native square planar stereoisomer structures and complete labels.
Complete cis/trans preparation schemes, all charges/reagents/intermediates, retaining native 2− intermediate.
Entire native Fig. 2.3 rate graph, axes/ticks/points/fit/constant annotations and printed reference caption.
Complete square planar substitution scheme showing ligand T trans to departing X and incoming Y.
Native two-step cisplatin preparation scheme, all ligands/charges/intermediates/reagents.
Native platinum bipy/pyridine substitution scheme with charge, CH₃OH, structures and chloride.
Full native gold-nanoparticle/oligonucleotide/PtIV illustration and three-item colour legend, intrinsically source-raster quality.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 3 — Thiomolybdates
problems.statement:
Thiomolybdate ions derive from molybdate MoO₄²⁻ by replacing oxygen with sulfur. They occur in deep Black Sea water where biological sulfate reduction generates H₂S. Transformation rapidly removes dissolved Mo from seawater into sediments, depleting an essential trace element. Relative concentrations in dilute solution obey:

MoS₄²⁻ + H₂O(l) ⇌ MoOS₃²⁻ + H₂S(aq), K₁ = 1.3×10⁻⁵.

MoOS₃²⁻ + H₂O(l) ⇌ MoO₂S₂²⁻ + H₂S(aq), K₂ = 1.0×10⁻⁵.

MoO₂S₂²⁻ + H₂O(l) ⇌ MoO₃S²⁻ + H₂S(aq), K₃ = 1.6×10⁻⁵.

MoO₃S²⁻ + H₂O(l) ⇌ MoO₄²⁻ + H₂S(aq), K₄ = 6.5×10⁻⁶.

parts.statement: At equilibrium [MoO₄²⁻] = 1×10⁻⁷ and [H₂S] = 1×10⁻⁶, find [MoS₄²⁻].
parts.statementAfter:
Solutions containing MoO₂S₂²⁻, MoOS₃²⁻ and MoS₄²⁻ absorb at 395/468 nm. Other ions and H₂S absorb negligibly. Molar absorptivities ε:

| Ion | ε468 / dm³ mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹ | ε395 / dm³ mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|
| MoS₄²⁻ | 11870 | 120 |
| MoOS₃²⁻ | 0 | 9030 |
| MoO₂S₂²⁻ | 0 | 3230 |

parts.statement: A nonequilibrium mixture contains only MoS₄²⁻, MoOS₃²⁻, MoO₂S₂²⁻ as Mo species, total 6.0×10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³. A 10.0 cm cell gives absorbances 0.365 at 468 nm and 0.213 at 395 nm. Calculate all three anion concentrations.
parts.statementAfter: Initial MoS₄²⁻ concentration 2.0×10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³ hydrolyzes in a closed system; H₂S accumulates to equilibrium. Calculate H₂S and all five Mo anion concentrations, ignoring possible H₂S → HS⁻ ionization. The printed parenthetic list is MoO₄²⁻, MoOS₃²⁻, MoO₂S₂²⁻, MoOS₃²⁻, MoS₄²⁻. Source note: its fourth species repeats MoOS₃²⁻; the preceding equilibria and key print MoO₃S²⁻.

parts.statement: Write six independent equations determining the system.
Calculate all six concentrations with reasonable approximations, giving two significant figures.

solution.statement:
**3.1** Multiply four mass-action laws: [MoO₄²⁻][H₂S]⁴/[MoS₄²⁻] = 10⁻⁷(10⁻⁶)⁴/[MoS₄²⁻] = 1.4×10⁻²⁰. Thus [MoS₄²⁻] = 7×10⁻¹².

**3.2** At 468 nm, 0.365 = 11870×10.0×c(MoS₄²⁻); c = 3.08×10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³. Mo conservation gives c(MoOS₃²⁻) + c(MoO₂S₂²⁻) = 6.0×10⁻⁶ − 3.08×10⁻⁶ = 2.9×10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³; hence c(MoO₂S₂²⁻) = 2.9×10⁻⁶ − c(MoOS₃²⁻).

At 395 nm (equation quantities without dimensions):

0.213 = (120×10.0×3.08×10⁻⁶) + (9030×10.0×c(MoOS₃²⁻)) + (3230×10.0×c(MoO₂S₂²⁻)).

Substitute the conservation relation: last term = 3230×10.0×(2.9×10⁻⁶ − c(MoOS₃²⁻)). Thus c(MoOS₃²⁻) = 2.0×10⁻⁶ and c(MoO₂S₂²⁻) = 0.9×10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³.

**3.3** Mo balance (1):

2.0×10⁻⁷ = c(MoS₄²⁻) + c(MoOS₃²⁻) + c(MoO₂S₂²⁻) + c(MoO₃S²⁻) + c(MoO₄²⁻).

S balance (2):

8.0×10⁻⁷ = 4c(MoS₄²⁻) + 3c(MoOS₃²⁻) + 2c(MoO₂S₂²⁻) + c(MoO₃S²⁻) + (H₂S).

Source notation: the last term is printed (H₂S) without c. Equilibrium relations (3)–(6):

1.3×10⁻⁵ = [MoOS₃²⁻][H₂S]/[MoS₄²⁻]; 1.0×10⁻⁵ = [MoO₂S₂²⁻][H₂S]/[MoOS₃²⁻]; 1.6×10⁻⁵ = [MoO₃S²⁻][H₂S]/[MoO₂S₂²⁻]; 6.5×10⁻⁶ = [MoO₄²⁻][H₂S]/[MoO₃S²⁻].

**3.4** Multiple approaches are possible. Maximum H₂S is 8.0×10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³ for complete hydrolysis. At this concentration MoO₃S²⁻ is about 12% of MoO₄²⁻ and remaining thio anions much less abundant. Two-significant-figure accuracy permits truncation:

2.0×10⁻⁷ = [MoO₃S²⁻] + [MoO₄²⁻] (Mo balance); 8.0×10⁻⁷ = [MoO₃S²⁻] + [H₂S] (S balance).

Subtract to obtain [MoO₄²⁻] = [H₂S] − 6.0×10⁻⁷; S balance gives [MoO₃S²⁻] = 8.0×10⁻⁷ − [H₂S].

6.5×10⁻⁶ = ([H₂S] − 6.0×10⁻⁷)[H₂S]/(8.0×10⁻⁷ − [H₂S]).

Rearrange and solve quadratically for H₂S, then back-substitute:

| Species | Concentration |
|---|---|
| H₂S | 7.8×10⁻⁷ |
| MoO₄²⁻ | 1.8×10⁻⁷ |
| MoO₃S²⁻ | 2.1×10⁻⁸ |
| MoO₂S₂²⁻ | 1.0×10⁻⁹ |
| MoOS₃²⁻ | 8.1×10⁻¹¹ |
| MoS₄²⁻ | 4.9×10⁻¹² |

problems.title: Theoretical problem 4 — Yttrium Barium Copper Oxide
problems.statement: In the 1980s ceramic materials showing superconductivity at unusually high 90 K were discovered. Yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO) contains Y, Ba, Cu, O. Nominal YBa₂Cu₃O₇ actually varies as YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ, 0 < δ < 0.5.

parts.statement:
Identify which circles in the idealized YBCO unit cell denote each element.

[figure: p4-fig1]

True structure is orthorhombic (a≠b≠c), approximately tetragonal with a≈b≈c/3.
YBCO δ = 0.25 gives lowest-angle CuKα X-ray diffraction peak 2θ = 7.450°, λ = 154.2 pm. Assuming a = b = c/3, calculate a and c.
Estimate this δ = 0.25 sample’s density in g cm⁻³. If 4.2 unsuccessful, use a = 500 pm, c = 1500 pm.
parts.statementAfter: Dissolving YBCO in aqueous HCl 1.0 mol dm⁻³ releases bubbles identified as O₂ by gas chromatography. Boiling 10 min expels dissolved gases. Excess KI then gives a yellow-brown solution titratable with thiosulfate to starch endpoint. Direct addition under Ar to 1.0 mol dm⁻³ both KI/HCl gives yellow-brown solution with no gas.

parts.statement: Write a balanced net ionic equation for solid YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ dissolving in HCl with O₂ evolution.
Write a balanced net ionic equation for the 4.4 solution reacting with excess KI in acid after dissolved oxygen is expelled.
Write a balanced net ionic equation for titration of 4.5 solution with thiosulfate S₂O₃²⁻.
Write a balanced net ionic equation for solid YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ dissolving in HCl/excess KI under Ar.
parts.statementAfter: Two identical unknown δ samples: first dissolves in 5 cm³ HCl 1.0 mol dm⁻³, evolves O₂; boil, cool, add 10 cm³ KI 0.7 mol dm⁻³ under Ar. Starch-endpoint titration consumes 1.542×10⁻⁴ mol thiosulfate. Second is added under Ar directly to 7 cm³ containing KI 1.0 mol dm⁻³/HCl 0.7 mol dm⁻³; titration consumes 1.696×10⁻⁴ mol thiosulfate.

parts.statement: Calculate the Cu amount in mol in each sample.
Calculate δ for these samples.

solution.statement:
**4.1** Native completed element legend:

[figure: p4-sol-fig1]

**4.2** sinθ = nλ/(2d). d = 154.2 pm/[2sin3.725°] = 1187 pm. Lowest angle gives longest spacing = c; c = 1187 pm, a = c/3 = 396 pm (native key repeats a = 396 pm).

**4.3** Vcell = a×b×c = 3a³ = 3(396 pm)³ = 1.863×10⁻²² cm³.

mcell = [88.91 + 2(137.33) + 3(63.55) + 6.75(16.00)]/NA = 662.22 g mol⁻¹/(6.0221×10²³ mol⁻¹) = 1.100×10⁻²¹ g.

Density = 1.100×10⁻²¹/1.863×10⁻²² = 5.90 g cm⁻³.

**4.4** YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ(s) + 13H⁺(aq) → Y³⁺(aq) + 2Ba²⁺(aq) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) + 0.25(1−2δ)O₂(g) + 6.5H₂O(l).

**4.5** 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 5I⁻(aq) → 2CuI(s) + I₃⁻(aq), or 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 4I⁻(aq) → 2CuI(s) + I₂(aq).

**4.6** I₃⁻(aq) + 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 3I⁻(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq), or I₂(aq) + 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 2I⁻(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq).

**4.7** YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ(s) + (14−2δ)H⁺(aq) + (9−3δ)I⁻(aq) → Y³⁺(aq) + 2Ba²⁺(aq) + 3CuI(s) + (7−δ)H₂O(l) + (2−δ)I₃⁻(aq), or YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ(s) + (14−2δ)H⁺(aq) + (7−2δ)I⁻(aq) → Y³⁺(aq) + 2Ba²⁺(aq) + 3CuI(s) + (7−δ)H₂O(l) + (2−δ)I₂(aq).

**4.8** n(Cu) = n(thiosulfate) in first titration = 1.542×10⁻⁴ mol.

**4.9** Total Cu 1.542×10⁻⁴ mol; CuIII = (1.696−1.542)×10⁻⁴ = 1.54×10⁻⁵ mol; 90% CuII, 10% CuIII. Charge balance:

2(7−δ) = 3 + 2(2) + 3[0.90(2) + 0.10(3)] = 13.30; δ = 0.35.

Alternatively, using balanced equations in (d): first titration each mole YBCO corresponds 1.5 mol I₃⁻/3 mol S₂O₃²⁻; second corresponds (2−δ) mol I₃⁻/(4−2δ) mol S₂O₃²⁻.

1.542×10⁻⁴ / 1.696×10⁻⁴ = 3/(4−2δ) = 1.5/(2−δ); 2−δ = 1.650; δ = 0.35.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 8 — Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons and Graphene
problems.statement:
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) occur as atmospheric pollutants, organic light-emitting-diode components and components of interstellar matter. Linear PAHs are one benzene ring wide with variable length; examples benzene, anthracene and pentacene are shown. Properties depend on π-electron delocalization.

[figure: p8-fig1]

parts.statement: Across benzene d = 240 pm. Estimate horizontal x-axis lengths da/dp of anthracene/pentacene.
parts.statementAfter:
Model benzene π electrons in a square, and conjugated PAH π electrons as free particles in a two-dimensional rectangular x–y box. Energies:

E = (nx²/Lx² + ny²/Ly²)h²/(8me).

nx/ny are independent integer quantum numbers1…∞, h is Planck’s constant, me electron mass, Lx/Ly box dimensions. Use this two-dimensional model for this problem.

parts.statement: Assume benzene x/y dimensions both d. Derive general linear-PAH quantized energies as a function of nx, ny, d, fused-ring count w, h and me.
parts.statementAfter:
Pentacene’s qualitative diagram gives all occupied π-electron levels and the lowest unoccupied level, labelled(nx;ny). Up/down arrows are opposite spins.

[figure: p8-fig2]

parts.statement:
Fill anthracene’s diagram with correct up/down electron arrows and nx/ny numbers in all blanks for occupied and lowest unoccupied levels. Some levels may have equal energy.

[figure: p8-fig3]

Create benzene’s energy-level diagram with occupied electrons and levels through the lowest unoccupied. Label every level(nx,ny). Do not assume this particle-in-a-square model gives the same levels as other models.
parts.statementAfter: PAH reactivity often correlates inversely with energy gap ΔE between highest occupied and lowest unoccupied levels.

parts.statement: Calculate ΔE in joules for benzene, anthracene and pentacene. Use8.3/8.4 for anthracene/benzene, or fallback highest-occupied(2,2)/lowest-unoccupied(3,2) for those two molecules (these may not be true values).
Rank benzene(B), anthracene(A), pentacene(P) in increasing reactivity by letters left-to-right in the box. Source gap: this referenced answer box is not printed.

Electronic absorption spectra (molar absorptivity versus wavelength) of anthracene(A), benzene(B), pentacene(P) are below. Use the particle-in-box model qualitatively to assign each spectrum in its box.

[figure: p8-fig4]
parts.statementAfter: Graphene is a sheet of carbon atoms in a two-dimensional honeycomb, an extreme PAH essentially infinite in both dimensions. The2010 Physics Nobel Prize recognized Andrei Geim/Konstantin Novoselov for graphene experiments. Consider Lx=Ly=25nm, with one hexagonal6-carbon unit area≈52400pm².

parts.statement:
Calculate π-electron count in a25nm×25nm graphene sheet. Ignore edge electrons outside full hexagons.

[figure: p8-fig5]
parts.statementAfter: Treat graphene π electrons as free electrons in a two-dimensional box. At large electron counts there is no single highest occupied level: many states with nearly equal energy are occupied and the rest empty. Highest occupied states define the Fermi level, containing multiple(nx,ny) combinations.

parts.statement:
Determine the25nm square’s Fermi energy relative to the lowest filled level, whose nonzero energy is negligible and may be taken as zero. Represent(nx,ny) states as grid points and fill with electron pairs. Use8.8 electron count or1000 (not necessarily the true value).

[figure: p8-fig6]

Graphene-like conductivity correlates inversely with its occupied/unoccupied energy gap. At a given temperature, is25nm×25nm graphene conductivity less than, equal to, or greater than1m×1m graphene (largest then obtained)? Circle: less / equal / greater.

solution.statement:
**8.1** da=3×240pm=720pm; dp=5×240pm=1200pm.

**8.2** E=(ny²/d² + nx²/(w²d²))h²/(8me) = (ny² + nx²/w²)h²/(8med²).

**8.3** Native anthracene diagram:

[figure: p8-sol-fig1]

Source note: its top row remains blank in the printed key; no unprinted numbers are supplied.

**8.4** Native benzene diagram:

[figure: p8-sol-fig2]

**8.5 — Benzene:** ΔE=E(2;2)−E(1;2)=3h²/(8med²)=3.14×10⁻¹⁸J. Alternate ΔE=E(3;2)−E(2;2)=5h²/(8med²)=5.23×10⁻¹⁸J.

**Anthracene:** ΔE=E(6;1)−E(2;2)=(5/9)h²/(8med²)=5.81×10⁻¹⁹J. Alternate ΔE=E(3;2)−E(2;2)=(5/9)h²/(8med²)=5.81×10⁻¹⁹J.

**Pentacene:** ΔE=E(3;2)−E(9;1)=(3/25)h²/(8med²)=1.26×10⁻¹⁹J.

**8.6** Least reactive B < A < P most reactive.

**8.7** Native assignments A/P/B:

[figure: p8-sol-fig3]

**8.8** Nunits=Areagraphene/Areaunit=(25000pm)²/52400pm²=12000. Each carbon belongs to three hexagons; each52400pm² unit contains6/3=2carbons contributing2π electrons.12000units contribute12000pairs. Correct answer24000π electrons.

**8.9** Two electrons fill each state;12000levels/pairs(nx,ny) are occupied. Lx=Ly and the lowest filled level is approximately zero:

ΔE=Ehighest=(nx²+ny²)h²/(8meLx²).

Circle rearrangement R²=nx²+ny²=E8meLx²/h²=constant.

[figure: p8-sol-fig4]

Area of occupied grid=πR²/4; quantum-pair area1. Therefore Npoints=Areagrid/Areapair=πR²/4=Nstates=12000.

Nstates=(π/4)(8meLx²E/h²)=12000; E=4h²×12000/(π8meLx²)=1.48×10⁻¹⁸J.

Alternate printed solution: Nstates=(π/4)(8meLx²E/h²)=1000; E=4h²×1000/(π8meLx²)=1.23×10⁻¹⁹J.

Source note: this alternative uses1000states, whereas8.9 fallback specifies1000electrons. Both native wording/result are preserved.

**8.10** Less. Increasing size reduces energy gaps and increases conductivity.
